lesson.title: Word Order & Subordinate Clauses
lesson.subtitle: Verb-second everywhere — until weil and dass slam the verb to the end

payoff.text: Here is the word that undoes it: weil (and its cousin dass). The moment one of them opens a clause, that clause's verb goes to the very end. Everything else about your sentence stays exactly as you learned it in topic 13.

hook.title: The Verb Has Two Homes
hook.content: German main clauses obey one law: the verb lives in position 2. Statement, fronted adverb, whatever — Ich lerne Deutsch. Morgen lerne ich Deutsch. The verb never moves. But walk through a door marked weil or dass and everything changes: the verb is thrown to the very end of the clause — Ich weiß, dass du kommst. Strange? Old English did the same: subordinate clauses parked their verbs late, and German never stopped. weil and dass are not foreign gadgets — dass is literally your that, and weil is your while wearing a new job title.

footnotes.title: weil Is while
footnotes.content: weil looks like a scholarly loan, but it is a plain descendant of the same Germanic word as English while — Proto-Germanic *hwīlō. It drifted from 'while' to 'because' ('for the while that...' → 'since/as' → 'because') while English kept the time sense.

pattern.title: Position 2, Then the Basement
pattern.content:
Main clause law: verb in position 2, no matter what fronts it — Morgen komme ich (Tomorrow, I come). Subordinate law: after weil, dass, wenn, the verb goes to the basement, the very last slot — Ich weiß, dass du Deutsch lernst. Ich lerne, weil ich will. Combine with your modal bracket and nothing new appears: Ich kann nicht kommen, weil ich arbeiten muss — a bracket inside a basement; the trapped verb muss waits at the very end.

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Ich kann nicht kommen, weil ich arbeiten muss → I can not come, because I must work → I can't come because I have to. Odd in English, exact in German — and Old English agreed with German about where the trapped verb waits.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “weil works like because, so the word order is free.” It is the opposite: weil sends the verb to the very end of its clause. The moment you see weil or dass, that clause's verb goes to the basement. Nothing else about your sentence changes — only the verb's seat moves.
pattern.linguist_note: dass ↔ that is a doublet of das: Proto-Germanic *þat. The spelling difference (das/dass) is a purely German orthographic convention — the two were one word in Old High German (daȥ) as in Old English (þæt).

exercises.prompt: Match each German clause structure with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: I know that you are coming
I learn because I want to
I know that the dog is big
matching_pairs.german: Ich weiß, dass der Hund groß ist

matching_pairs.english: I know that you have worry
matching_pairs.german: Ich weiß, dass du Sorge hast

exercises.target_answer: Ich weiß, dass du kommst, Ich lerne, weil ich will, Ich weiß, dass der Hund groß ist, Ich weiß, dass du Sorge hast, Ich kenne niemanden, Ich weiß nichts, Ich kenne deine Meinung, Gleich komme ich, Ich komme nie
exercises.meaning: I know that you are coming, I learn because I want to, I know that the dog is big, I know that you have worry, I know nobody, I know nothing, I know your opinion, I'm coming right away, I never come
exercises.explanation: Main clauses keep the verb in position 2; dass and weil throw it to the end of their clause. kennen is 'to know a person or thing' — it takes your new nouns along for free.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.german: Ich weiß, dass es dunkel ist.
exercises.natural: I know that it is dark.
options: I know that it is dark.
I know that it dark is.
I know that is it dark.
exercises.target_answer: I know that it dark is.
exercises.meaning: I know that it is dark.
exercises.explanation: Read it the German way first: 'I know that it dark is.' dass slams the conjugated verb to the end of its clause — Old English's own habit, which German never gave up. The third option over-flips: only the subclause verb waits, never the main one.

exercises.prompt: Fronting 'Gleich' (right away) in a statement: 'Gleich _____ ich.'
exercises.meaning: Gleich komme ich — the verb holds position 2
exercises.explanation: When an adverb takes position 1, the verb stays glued to position 2 and the subject slides to third.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Ich weiß dass du Deutsch lernst
exercises.target_answer: Ich weiß dass du Deutsch lernst
exercises.meaning: I know that you are learning German
cues: In the basement the verb waits at the very end: lernst
exercises.explanation: After dass the conjugated verb sinks to the very end. Two clauses, one architecture: weiß holds position 2 in the first, lernst waits at the door of the second.
exercises.affirmation: You heard the basement — the verb at the very end is the sound of a dass-clause.

exercises.idea: you're reporting on the neighborhood's most punctual animal — you know one thing for sure: the cat is coming. Say it with that.
cues: Main clause first: Ich weiß — verb in position 2
dass opens the basement: die Katze (the cat, feminine), and kommt waits at the very end
exercises.target_answer: Ich weiß dass die Katze kommt
exercises.meaning: I know that the cat is coming

vocab_hints.note: the exact twin of English that — and it sends the verb to the end
die Katze — feminine flag, unchanged in the accusative

exercises.explanation: Main clause verb (weiß) in position 2; after dass, the subclause verb (kommt) waits in the basement — Old English's own habit.

diagnosis.cue: dass slams the conjugated verb to the end of its clause — die Katze kommt, with kommt last. The basement is the law.

summary.outcome: Build verb-second main clauses and verb-final weil/dass subclauses.

use_example.german: Ich weiß, dass die Katze kommt.
use_example.english: I know that the cat is coming.

summary.takeaway: Verb in position 2 in main clauses; after weil and dass it waits in the basement — Old English's own habit.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the verb-second bootcamp — front adverbs and objects while the verb stays glued to position 2.

twist.prompt: Basement check: she knows one thing about you — you like the animal. Fold it under dass: she knows that I like the animal.
twist.target_answer: Sie weiß dass ich das Tier mag
twist.explanation: Two clauses, two laws: weiß holds position 2 in the main clause; after dass, mag sinks to the basement's last slot. The person changed — the architecture didn't.

weil.context_translation: I learn because I want to.
weil.etymology_derivation: Not a Latin loan: a plain descendant of Proto-Germanic *hwīlō — the same word as English while. [wiktionary]

dass.context_translation: I know that you are coming.
dass.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *þat — the exact twin of English that, and a doublet of German das. [wiktionary]

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

sorge.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *surgo — the page lists English sorrow as the cognate: the same care-root that grew into sorrow. [wiktionary]

gleich.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, having the same form, built from ga- plus the ancestor of -like; the English twin is alike, and the suffix inside it is the same element as English -like and -ly. [wiktionary]

meinung.context_phrase: Meiner Meinung nach ist der Film gut.
meinung.context_translation: In my opinion the film is good.
meinung.etymology_derivation: meinen (to mean) + -ung; the page compares English meaning — your opinion is what you mean. [wiktionary]

nie.context_phrase: Ich habe nie Zeit am Montag.
nie.context_translation: I never have time on Monday.
nie.etymology_derivation: MHG nie, OHG nio; thin etymology on Wiktionary. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

nichts.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German nihtes niht, literally nothing of nothing — an emphatic doubling of niht 'not', just like French rien de rien. [wiktionary]

niemand.etymology_derivation: nie 'never' + Mann 'man': literally never-man — the page analyzes it exactly so, the same idea as English no man and none. [wiktionary]

katze.context_phrase: Die Katze schläft auf dem Sofa.
katze.context_translation: The cat sleeps on the sofa.

hund.context_phrase: Der Hund schläft auf dem Sofa.
hund.context_translation: The dog sleeps on the sofa.
hund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaz — cognate with English hound, the same ancient dog-word. [wiktionary]

kennen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *kannijaną, a causative of *kunnaną (can); the page lists English ken (as in beyond my ken) — the same knowing-verb English keeps in Scotland. [wiktionary]

tier.etymology_derivation: From Old High German tior, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from PIE *dʰewsóm. English deer is the listed cognate; the Germanic d appears as t in High German. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
